extracted.intended_audience: film marketers, students, journalists, and general readers interested in film promotion
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of techniques, channels, and research used to promote films (press junkets, advertising, merchandising, interviews, audience research) and practical guidance on execution and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film promotion components
rubrics_metrics.description: Film promotion generally includes press releases, advertising campaigns, merchandising, franchising, media, and interviews with the key people involved in making the film, such as the film's actors and directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerates the principal vehicles used in coordinating promotion with distribution; these components form the baseline activities studios invest in to maximize revenue early in the release cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing budget scale and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing budgets tend to equal about half the production budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of high financial risk, film studios invest in expensive marketing campaigns to maximize revenue early in the release cycle; timing is important since films typically don’t linger in theaters more than 4–6 weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity is generally handled by the distributor and exhibitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution and exhibition partners are typically responsible for managing publicity efforts and media relations around a release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trailers and teasers as primary promotional tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Trailers, teaser are a mainstay of film promotion because they are delivered directly to movie-goers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trailers are presented in theaters or on TV/online, generally telling the story in a highly condensed fashion and compressing maximum appeal into roughly two and a half minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-theater display materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use film posters, slideshows (stills, trivia, trivia games between showtimes), standees (life-size paperboard images), and cardboard 3D displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These materials are designed to reach captive audiences at point-of-exhibition and can include sound or interactive elements to increase impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gimmicks to enhance viewing experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Gimmicks that enhance the viewing experience by incorporating unusual or novel elements into otherwise regular films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include live effects and performances corresponding to in-film events, scratch-and-sniff cards, and various levels of interactivity; used to create a memorable, differentiated theatrical event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television and radio advertising deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Hollywood distributors spend heavily on paid advertising (30-second TV commercials, magazine/newspaper ads), with over half the total placed on broadcast and cable TV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TV is effective as an audio-visual medium to deliver a vast audience quickly; heavy upfront buys matter because theatrical windows are short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product placement and extended placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Product placement: paid active or passive insertion of film branding in other programming; Extended placement: full episodes or segments devoted to compensated exposure of the film, stars, clips, director, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement can be passive (on-set props) or active (plot mentions); extended placements can appear on talk shows, entertainment news, or network news for deeper exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews and broadcast appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews with actors and directors (often filmed in hotel junkets) are featured on local news, cable networks, and entertainment programs to generate stories and 'marketing buzz.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews should encourage journalists to publish exclusives; interviewees are expected to stay 'on message', disclose enough behind-the-scenes detail to offer a scoop, and tactfully avoid embarrassing or negative information that could harm box office or reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behind-the-scenes and documentary-style programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Production and paid broadcast of behind-the-scenes documentary-style shows produced for premium channels and long-form outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These deepen audience engagement and can be used as longer-form publicity vehicles on HBO, Showtime, Starz, or similar platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet marketing strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of standalone studio-sponsored websites, virtual relationship hyperlink marketing, online digital film screeners, viral marketing (free distribution of trailers and rapid dissemination via email/blogs), and social media marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include bait-and-switch hyperlink articles, secure streaming screeners with expiry controls, viral leaks of 'rushes' or early trailers, YouTube shorts/series preceding release, paid online ads, and coordinated social campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of early/alternate online content
rubrics_metrics.description: Using original short films or other online content (e.g., YouTube shorts) in the lead-up to a feature's premiere to build awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-lead content or episodic shorts can build an audience while the film is in production; example: The Muppets used original shorts released over years prior to the film's premiere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print advertising and cross-promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Paid advertisement in newspapers, magazines, inserts in books, cross-promotion of original books/novelizations, comic special editions or special episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print placements and tie-in publications extend reach to readers and fandoms; 'Now a major motion picture' branding can drive book sales and awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchandising and co-branding
rubrics_metrics.description: Paid co-branding or co-advertising of a product with the film, promotional giveaways (branded drink cups, toys, fast-food combos), and experiential promotions (e.g., life-sized branded environments rentable via Airbnb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merchandising creates ancillary revenue and extends brand visibility; co-brand deals (e.g., Aston Martin and James Bond) align film prestige with consumer products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional tours and press junkets
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors, directors, and producers travel on promotional tours, sit for dozens of interviews, and appear in media to generate buzz; often grueling for international distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants are often contracted to travel to multiple cities; they must remain energetic, on-message, provide just enough scoop, and avoid disclosures that could harm box office performance or critical reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience research as a strategic pillar
rubrics_metrics.description: There are seven distinct types of research conducted by film distributors for domestic theatrical releases: positioning studies, test screenings, testing of advertising materials, tracking surveys, exit surveys, title testing, and concept testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such research can cost $1 million per film and is primarily used by major studios to shape promotional materials; independents often lack the budget. Research informs positioning vs. competing films and drives iterative changes to marketing up to opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of audience research (detailed)
rubrics_metrics.description: When audience research is conducted it involves: positioning studies versus other films; test screenings of finished or nearly finished films; testing audience response to advertising materials; tracking surveys beginning six weeks before premiere; exit surveys about demographics and marketing effectiveness; title testing at an early stage; concept testing during development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each research type targets a different decision point (development, title selection, advertising creative, campaign tracking, and post-experience feedback) and collectively informs marketing strategy and green-light considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing's influence on green-light decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing can play a big role in whether or not a film gets the green light; audience research is a strong factor in determining the ability of a film to sell in theaters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and studios consider marketability and research outcomes when deciding to proceed with production; promotional materials evolve based on research findings through release.
